title: Since Thursday
setting: A patient describes four days of illness in the wrong order.

lines.t: It started on Thursday. I think I've come down with something.
Tell me the symptoms in the order they appeared.
Headache first, then the cough, then a temperature last night.
Is the cough new, or is it the chronic one we talked about in winter?
This one is different. It came on suddenly.
So it's acute. Your medical history says the same thing happened in February.
Twice a year, every year.
That pattern matters more than this week does. Are you allergic to anything?
Penicillin, I think. My mother says so.
Then we check it properly before any diagnosis turns into a prescription. 'I think' isn't good enough with penicillin.

title: Before we guess
setting: A reading was high twice and the patient has an explanation ready.

lines.t: Before we guess at anything, I'd like to run some tests.
Is something wrong?
Probably nothing. Your blood pressure was high both times I took it.
It's always high at the doctor's.
That happens to a lot of people. So we'll take your blood pressure at home, twice a day for a week.
And the rest?
A blood test tomorrow morning, before you eat anything.
My brother had a scan for this.
A scan answers a different question. We start with the blood test and see what it tells us.
How long for the results?
Four days. If anything needs attention sooner, you'll hear from me the same day.

title: You're due
setting: A nurse persuades a healthy patient to come in anyway.

lines.t: You're due for two things. A check-up, and the flu vaccination.
I feel perfectly well.
That's the best time to come.
Is the vaccination necessary at my age?
At your age it matters more than it did at forty.
And the check-up?
Twenty minutes. Blood pressure, weight, a few questions, and a blood test if anything looks unusual.
My neighbour says the screening letter is only paperwork.
Your neighbour's screening letter found something early two years ago, which is why she's still here complaining about paperwork.
Put me down for Thursday.

title: Finish the course
setting: A patient who always stops taking medicine as soon as he feels better.

lines.t: The infection is bacterial, so antibiotics will help.
For how long?
Seven days. The prescription is ready at the desk, and the dosage is on the box: one tablet, three times a day, with food.
I usually stop when I feel better.
That's how the next infection becomes harder to treat. Finish the course.
Any side effects?
Some people feel sick for the first two days. If a rash appears, stop and call me.
And for the pain?
A painkiller when you need one. Once it wears off after four hours you can take another.
The surgeon mentioned an operation.
If the antibiotics work, nobody has to operate on anything. Surgery is the plan we'd rather not reach for.
And if you do reach for it?
Two nights in hospital, physiotherapy afterwards, and a rehabilitation programme for six weeks. People your age recover well, and the injection you had today buys us time to decide.

title: Two minutes at the bedside
setting: A junior doctor asks a patient why he has stopped eating.

lines.t: Good morning. I noticed you haven't eaten since yesterday.
I'm not very hungry.
Your tests are all normal, so I wondered if something else was wrong.
It's silly, really.
Tell me anyway. I have two minutes and nowhere else to be.
If I eat, I'll need the toilet. I can't reach it on my own.
And you didn't want to trouble the nurses.
They're busy. So I thought I'd manage until I go home.
Let me move your call bell closer, and I'll tell the ward.
That's all it takes? Then I'll have lunch.

title: Bed eleven
setting: A handover at the end of a shift, with a frightened relative waiting.

lines.t: Bed eleven on the ward. He came in at four this morning.
Who admitted him?
His GP sent him in, and triage put him near the front.
Is he staying, or is he an outpatient?
Staying. The consultant sees him at eleven.
Which consultant?
Dr Petrova. She's on call until eight tonight.
Then she'll be asleep at eleven.
She's doing the ward round anyway. My shift ends at seven, so I'll hand him over to Rada.
Tell her about the daughter. She's frightened and she keeps asking everybody the same question.
I've explained it twice already.
Explain it a third time, slowly. Bedside manner is most of what she'll remember about this week, and we can't discharge him until somebody at home understands the medication.

title: The waiting list
setting: A manager shows a consultant why capacity is being lost.

lines.t: The waiting list is nine months. You asked for two more staff.
Because we can't see enough patients.
Eighteen per cent of appointments are no-shows.
That's higher than I thought.
And twelve per cent arrive without a referral, so they're turned away.
Almost a third of the capacity, before anyone is treated.
A text message two days before, and a check when booking.
And a short-notice list for slots that open up.
Exactly. No new staff, no new equipment.
I've been treating a process problem as a resource problem for three years.

title: The letter that never came
setting: Six weeks after an appointment, nobody has been in touch.

lines.t: I was told I'd get a referral six weeks ago.
Let me open your patient record.
Nobody has called me.
The referral went out on the 9th. You're on the waiting list at the hospital, position fourteen.
Fourteen. How long is that?
About three months for that clinic.
And with health insurance?
Three weeks, if your policy covers it. Bring the card and we'll check together.
I also need something for work.
A sick note for the days you've already missed, and the doctor signs it today.
My sick leave runs out at the end of the month.
Then let's book the follow-up appointment now, before the book fills. And nothing happens here without informed consent, so read whatever you sign.

title: Somebody call an ambulance
setting: A man has collapsed in a corridor and two people are deciding what to do.

lines.t: He's on the floor in the corridor and he isn't answering me.
Call an ambulance now. Say the address twice and don't hang up.
Should I move him?
Leave him where he is. Is he breathing?
I can't tell.
Put your ear next to his mouth and watch his chest. Ten seconds.
Nothing.
Then I start CPR and you keep the line open. Tell them it's life-threatening, in exactly those words.
The first aid box is in the kitchen.
Leave it. Send somebody to the front door so the crew from A&E find us in seconds instead of minutes.
